title: NumPy Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the NumPy lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Make a number array
entries.summary: A NumPy array holds values with a shared data type. np.array builds one from a Python list.

example.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(scores.tolist())

notes: Do not confuse an array with one single number.

entries.name: Read the shape
entries.summary: Shape tells you the size of each dimension. A table-like array has a row count and a column count.

example.code:
import numpy as np

grid = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(grid.shape)

notes: The first shape number is not always the total number of values.

entries.name: Choose a data type
entries.summary: A data type describes how values are stored. An explicit type avoids guessing when size or precision matters.

example.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.float32)
print(values.dtype)

notes: Floating-point values cannot represent every decimal fraction exactly.

entries.name: Index a position
entries.summary: An index selects a position. NumPy, like Python lists, starts counting at zero.

example.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([5, 7, 9])
print(values[1])

notes: Index 3 is outside this three-value array.

entries.name: Slice a range
entries.summary: A slice selects a range. Its starting index is included and its stopping index is excluded.

example.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])
print(values[1:3].tolist())

notes: Basic slicing often gives a view of the original data, not an independent copy.

entries.name: Calculate element by element
entries.summary: Adding two arrays of the same shape adds matching positions. This is element-wise addition.

example.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print((a + b).tolist())

notes: Array addition is not the same as joining two Python lists.

entries.name: Broadcast one value
entries.summary: Broadcasting lets some differently shaped values work together. A single number can be used for every item in an array.

example.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print((scores + 1).tolist())

notes: Not every pair of shapes can broadcast; their dimensions must follow NumPy's rules.

entries.name: Sum along an axis
entries.summary: An axis is one direction through an array. For this two-dimensional table, axis 0 combines rows to produce a total for each column.

example.code:
import numpy as np

grid = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(grid.sum(axis=0).tolist())

notes: Draw the table before choosing an axis if the direction is confusing.

entries.name: Reshape without changing the count
entries.summary: reshape changes the arrangement of values. The new shape must hold the same total number of values.

example.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
print(values.reshape(2, 3).tolist())

notes: You cannot reshape six values into a full 2 by 2 table.

entries.name: Filter with a boolean mask
entries.summary: A boolean mask is a list of true-or-false choices. True positions are kept when used to select array values.

example.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([3, 8, 5])
mask = scores >= 5
print(scores[mask].tolist())

notes: Use element-wise logical operators carefully; normal Python and/or do not combine whole array masks.

entries.name: Make an independent copy
entries.summary: A copy owns separate data. It is useful when changing a result must not change the original array.

example.code:
import numpy as np

original = np.array([1, 2, 3])
copy = original.copy()
copy[0] = 99
print(original.tolist())

notes: Assigning copy = original only gives the same array another name.

entries.name: Summarise a small dataset
entries.summary: The mean is the total divided by the number of values. The minimum and maximum describe the range.

example.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(float(scores.mean()), int(scores.min()), int(scores.max()))

notes: One average can hide important differences between individual values.
